# Day of China — full text

> One ordinary day in China, from 6:30 a.m. to 9 p.m.

Day of China
A Day in the Life of a Chinese Person
Learn Chinese culture the way it is actually lived —
one ordinary day at a time
. From morning Ba Duan Jin and Tai Chi in the park to a foot soak before bed, this is a day in the life of a Chinese person. Our
first guide
is on its way.
One day, eleven moments
No lectures, no lists of dynasties. Just a day — the way millions of Chinese people still live it, timed to the old twelve two-hour periods, from 卯时 at dawn to 亥时 at night.
6:30
Ba Duan Jin and Tai Chi in the park
卯时 · 5–7 · 大肠经当令
The day starts slowly, in the park, moving with the neighbours.
八段锦
(bā duàn jǐn) — the Eight Brocades, eight gentle stretches to wake the body — followed by
太极
(tài jí), Tai Chi, slow and flowing, breath and balance.
7:30
Make breakfast — noodles and dough, by hand
辰时 · 7–9 · 胃经当令
Breakfast is made, not bought. Hand-pulled noodles,
面食
(miànshí), steamed
包子
(bāozi) buns, warm soy milk, and a bowl of congee,
粥
(zhōu).
9:00
Brew health tea, by hand
巳时 · 9–11 · 脾经当令
A pot of tea,
茶
(chá), blended for the season — a health tea,
养生茶
(yǎngshēng chá), made yourself. Then a book, and a brush: calligraphy,
书法
(shūfǎ), is practice — not performance.
10:30
The wet market
巳时 · 9–11 · 脾经当令
Picking vegetables by hand, bargaining a little, knowing the vendors by name. The
菜市场
(càishìchǎng) is where dinner begins.
11:00
Cook lunch — cold dishes and stir-fry
午时 · 11–13 · 心经当令
A cold dish,
凉菜
(liángcài), and a hot stir-fry,
炒菜
(chǎocài). Two or three dishes, cooked fresh.
12:00
Lunch with family
午时 · 11–13 · 心经当令
Rice, two or three dishes, and everyone at the table. Lunch is a family meal, not a desk meal.
13:00
Nap
午时 · 11–13 · 子午觉
A short midday rest,
午休
(wǔxiū) — the midday half of the old 子午觉, the two sleeps of the day. The whole country slows down for an hour.
15:00
Afternoon tea, Go, chess, a stroll
申时 · 15–17 · 膀胱经当令
Another pot of tea, a game of Go,
围棋
(wéiqí), or Chinese chess,
象棋
(xiàngqí), and a slow walk around the block.
16:00
Start the soup — seasonal, by the solar terms
申时 · 15–17 · 膀胱经当令
A soup,
煲汤
(bāotāng), simmers for hours — it is care, cooked slowly. The recipe follows the twenty-four solar terms,
二十四节气
(èrshísì jiéqì): what simmers in summer is not what simmers in winter.
18:30
Dinner, family chat
酉时 · 17–19 · 肾经当令
The soup is on the table, the dishes are served. The table fills up again, and the day is talked over, dish by dish.
21:00
Foot soak, early sleep
亥时 · 21–23 · 三焦经当令
Hot water,
泡脚
(pàojiǎo) — a foot soak — and an early night, asleep before 子时 (11 p.m.). Tomorrow starts at 6:30 again.
What is Day of China?
Day of China is a small guide to Chinese traditional culture — taught the way it is lived, not the way it is listed in textbooks. Each guide follows one day: Ba Duan Jin, Tai Chi, tea, calligraphy, cooking, Go, and the quiet habits in between — timed to the old twelve two-hour periods, 十二时辰.
The first guide,
A Day in the Life of a Chinese Person
, is coming soon.

## Ba Duan Jin and Tai Chi in the park
https://dayofchina.com/moments/ba-duan-jin-tai-chi/

Ba Duan Jin and Tai Chi in the park — Day of China
Home
Moments
Guides
About
Home
/
Moments
/ 6:30
6:30
· 卯时 · 5–7 · 大肠经当令
Ba Duan Jin and Tai Chi in the park
The day starts slowly, in the park, moving with the neighbours.
What happens
Before the shops open and the traffic starts, the park is already full. Neighbours gather in loose groups on the paved clearings — some in their sixties and seventies, some younger, a few with grandchildren in tow. Nobody is in a hurry. The movements are slow and unshowy: arms rising, torsos turning, weight shifting from one foot to the other. This is 晨练 (chén liàn), the morning exercise — a daily habit for millions of Chinese people, and the first moment of the day.
Why this hour
The old day-clock divides the day into twelve two-hour periods, each paired with an organ system. 卯时 (mǎo shí), 5–7 a.m., belongs to the large intestine. In the traditional view, this is the hour when the body clears out the night — which is why the morning starts with movement and warm water, before breakfast. Whether or not you follow the old medicine, the logic is plain: move first, eat second.
Try it
Wake before 7 and drink a cup of warm water.
Find a park, a square, or any open ground near home.
Do the Eight Brocades — eight gentle stretches: Two Hands Hold Up the Heavens; Draw the Bow to Shoot the Eagle; Raise One Arm to Regulate the Spleen and Stomach; Look Back to Cure the Five Strains and Seven Injuries; Shake the Head and Wag the Tail to Calm the Heart; Hold the Feet to Strengthen the Kidneys and Waist; Clench the Fists and Glare to Build Strength; Bounce on the Heels to Dispel Illness.
Follow with a few minutes of Tai Chi: slow, flowing, breath and balance.
Walk home and eat breakfast.
Words to know
八段锦 (bā duàn jǐn)
The Eight Brocades — eight gentle stretches.
太极 (tài jí)
Tai Chi — the Supreme Ultimate; slow, flowing movement.
卯时 (mǎo shí)
5–7 a.m. — the first two-hour period of the working day.
晨练 (chén liàn)
Morning exercise — the daily park habit.
Questions
What's the difference between Ba Duan Jin and Tai Chi?
Ba Duan Jin is a fixed set of eight stretches — qigong, or energy exercise. Tai Chi is a flowing sequence of connected movements, originally a martial art. Many people do both: stretches first to wake the body, then Tai Chi. Neither needs equipment.
Do I need a teacher to start?
A teacher helps with posture, but you can start from a video. Learn the eight stretches one at a time, slowly, and don't force any movement that hurts.
What time do people go?
Around 6:30, before breakfast. Parks fill up at dawn and empty out by 8, when the day's work starts.
Is it only for older people?
The dawn crowd in Chinese parks skews older, but all ages practise. Morning exercise is a habit, not an age group.
What should I wear?
Flat shoes and loose clothes. That's all.
Go deeper
The full morning routine — the eight stretches in order, with pictures and a printable practice sheet — is in our first guide,
Tai Chi & Ba Duan Jin
($9.99, coming soon).

## The wet market
https://dayofchina.com/moments/wet-market/

The wet market — Day of China
Home
Moments
Guides
About
Home
/
Moments
/ 10:30
10:30
· 巳时 · 9–11 · 脾经当令
The wet market
Picking vegetables by hand, bargaining a little, knowing the vendors by name.
What happens
By 10:30 the market is in full swing. Stalls of leafy greens, baskets of eggs, tanks of live fish, pork hanging from hooks. Vendors call out the day's prices; regulars stop at the same stalls they stopped at yesterday, and the vendors know them by name. Nothing is wrapped in plastic. You pick vegetables up with your hands, turn them over, and ask what's fresh today. The 菜市场 (càishìchǎng) is where dinner begins — not in a fridge, not in a delivery app.
Why this hour
The market run sits in 巳时 (sì shí), 9–11 a.m. — the spleen's hours in the old clock. In the traditional view, late morning belongs to digestion and nourishment: the body is turning breakfast into energy, and the day's food is bought now, fresh, so lunch can be cooked from it. Shopping daily, not weekly, is the point.
Try it
Go before 11 — the fullest stalls, the freshest pick.
Walk the whole market once before buying anything.
Buy what's in season — ask the vendor “现在什么新鲜？” (What's fresh now?).
Bargain lightly: ask the price, offer a little less, settle with a smile. Small amounts, small talk — not a battle.
Buy for today only. Fresh, daily, nothing stored.
Words to know
菜市场 (càishìchǎng)
Wet market — the open fresh-food market.
讲价 (jiǎng jià)
To bargain, to haggle — lightly, with a smile.
新鲜 (xīn xiān)
Fresh — the first word to learn in any market.
摊主 (tān zhǔ)
Stall keeper — the person who knows your name by day three.
Questions
What is a wet market?
An open market selling fresh meat, fish, and vegetables. “Wet” because the floors are washed down through the day and the produce is fresh, not packaged.
Do vendors speak English?
Usually very little. Pointing, a calculator, and a smile go a long way — and the numbers are always shown, not just spoken.
How do I bargain without offending?
Ask the price first, then offer a little less and meet in the middle. Keep it light: small amounts, a smile, and accept the final price gracefully. Don't bargain hard over a few mao.
Cash or phone payment?
Phone payment (WeChat Pay or Alipay) is the norm in Chinese cities now. Cash still works, but small vendors may not have change for large notes.
When is the best time to go?
Early morning has the fullest stalls. 10:30 is when the day's shopping happens — late enough to be unhurried, early enough that nothing is picked over.
Go deeper
What you buy here becomes lunch — cooked at 11:00, the next moment in the day. See
all eleven moments
.

## Start the soup
https://dayofchina.com/moments/simmering-soup/

Start the soup — seasonal, by the solar terms — Day of China
Home
Moments
Guides
About
Home
/
Moments
/ 16:00
16:00
· 申时 · 15–17 · 膀胱经当令
Start the soup — seasonal, by the solar terms
A soup simmers for hours — it is care, cooked slowly.
What happens
At four in the afternoon, the soup goes on. Meat or bones, a few dried ingredients, cold water in a clay pot — then hours of the gentlest simmer. Nobody watches it. It just sits there on the lowest flame, doing its work, while the afternoon goes on around it. 煲汤 (bāo tāng) is care, cooked slowly: the point is not speed but extraction, and the recipe follows the twenty-four solar terms — what simmers in summer is not what simmers in winter.
Why this hour
Soup starts in 申时 (shēn shí), 3–5 p.m. — the bladder's hours in the old clock, the water hours. The traditional view pairs the afternoon with water and rest before the evening meal. The practical reason is the same: a soup that needs hours must start now to be on the table at 18:30.
Try it
Pick a soup for the season — light and clear in summer, richer with root vegetables in winter.
Start with cold water and bring it to a boil, then skim off the foam.
Turn the heat to the lowest simmer and leave it for 2–3 hours.
Salt at the end, not the start.
Serve with dinner — the soup started at 16:00 is on the table at 18:30.
Words to know
煲汤 (bāo tāng)
Slow-simmered soup — hours on the lowest flame.
二十四节气 (èr shí sì jié qì)
The twenty-four solar terms — the old farming calendar that decides the recipe.
火候 (huǒ hòu)
Heat control — the knack of the flame.
砂锅 (shā guō)
Clay pot — the traditional soup pot.
Questions
How is 煲汤 different from ordinary soup?
Time. A quick soup is boiled and served; 煲汤 simmers for hours on the lowest flame. The point is slow extraction — flavour and nourishment drawn out gradually.
What goes into a seasonal soup?
It follows the twenty-four solar terms. Summer soups are light and clearing; winter soups are richer, often with root vegetables and dried ingredients. The season decides, not the cook's whim.
Do I need a special pot?
A clay pot (砂锅) is traditional because it holds gentle heat well. Any heavy pot with a lid works — the low flame matters more than the pot.
When do you eat it?
With dinner. The soup started at 16:00 is on the table at 18:30, alongside the dishes.
Is soup a dish or a drink?
Both. It arrives with the meal and is eaten with it — sipped from a small bowl between bites, not as a starter and not as an afterthought.
Go deeper
The soup is on the table at dinner, 18:30 — the next moment in the day. See
all eleven moments
.

## About
https://dayofchina.com/about/

About — Day of China
Home
Moments
Guides
About
Home
/ About
What is Day of China?
A small guide to Chinese traditional culture — taught the way it is lived, not the way it is listed in textbooks.
One day, not one encyclopedia
Each guide follows one day: Ba Duan Jin, Tai Chi, tea, calligraphy, cooking, Go, and the quiet habits in between — timed to the old twelve two-hour periods, 十二时辰 (shí'èr shíchén).
The first guide,
A Day in the Life of a Chinese Person
, is coming soon. The
eleven moments
are already on the site; the
printable guides
follow one moment at a time.
Who it's for
Curious beginners — English readers who know little about China and want to understand how ordinary Chinese people actually live a day. No background needed, no lectures, no lists of dynasties.
How the day works: the twelve two-hour periods
The old Chinese day is divided into twelve periods of two hours, each paired with an organ system in traditional medicine. The site's eleven moments are timed to it.
Period
Hours
Organ system (traditional view)
子
11 p.m.–1 a.m.
Gallbladder
丑
1–3 a.m.
Liver
寅
3–5 a.m.
Lungs
卯
5–7 a.m.
Large intestine
辰
7–9 a.m.
Stomach
巳
9–11 a.m.
Spleen
午
11 a.m.–1 p.m.
Heart
未
1–3 p.m.
Small intestine
申
3–5 p.m.
Bladder
酉
5–7 p.m.
Kidneys
戌
7–9 p.m.
Pericardium
亥
9–11 p.m.
Triple burner
A note on accuracy
Everything on this site is public, checkable fact or clearly labelled tradition. Where we describe the old medicine — the twelve periods, the solar terms — we describe what the tradition says, not medical advice.
